parts.title_ru: Часть 1 — хук, детство и рождение IKEA

beats.text: A young man is trying to squeeze a little table into his small car... and it just won't go in.
So he does something simple. He takes the legs off.
That small, frustrated moment would shape the business model of a brand whose stores now sell more than forty-four billion euros of home furnishings a year.
But this story starts long before that table... with a farm boy selling matches. So how does a kid on a bicycle build all this?
This is How They Built It. I'm Mila Sterling... and today, we're telling the story of IKEA.
Sweden, the nineteen-thirties. On a farm called Elmtaryd, near the village of Agunnaryd, lives a boy named Ingvar Kamprad.
beats.chapter: A Boy Who Loved to Sell

beats.text: This is Smaland. Stony, poor land... so poor that whole villages left for America. The Kamprad farm is big, mostly forest... yet money is tight.
But Ingvar has a talent the farm can't teach... he loves to sell.
In 1931, at just five years old, he starts selling matches to the neighbors.
Then his aunt in Stockholm helps with a trick. She buys matches in bulk, at a wholesale price... and posts them to him.
Ingvar sells them one box at a time, at a low price... and still makes a profit. At five.
Soon he's selling fish he caught himself... then Christmas decorations, seeds and pencils, from his bicycle, farm to farm.
Buy cheap, sell cheap... and still make money. Remember that. One day, it's going to save his company.
In 1943, at just seventeen, Ingvar registers his own company. But he's still a minor... so he needs a signature.
He cycles to his guardian, a man he calls uncle Ernst. Ernst can't see why a boy needs a company... but he signs.
Now he needs a name, so he uses his initials. I and K, for Ingvar Kamprad. E, for Elmtaryd, the farm. And the letter A... for Agunnaryd, the village.
IKEA.
There's just one strange thing. For its first five years... this company won't sell a single piece of furniture.

parts.title_ru: Часть 2 — почта, шоурум и плоская упаковка

beats.text: Instead, IKEA starts as a mail-order business, run from the family farm.
Pens, wallets, picture frames, watches, nylon stockings... whatever people need, at a low price.
And delivery? Every morning, the milk lorry that collects the farm's milk takes Ingvar's parcels too.
Milk churns and IKEA parcels on the same truck... until there are so many that the dairy says no more.
Then, in 1948, he adds a few easy chairs and tables, made cheaply by small workshops in Smaland's forests... and they sell.
In 1951, the first IKEA catalogue goes out... two hundred and eighty-five thousand copies, across southern Sweden.
A year later, he goes all in. From now on, IKEA will sell only furniture and home furnishings.
But there's a problem. Customers buy by mail... they can't see or touch what they're paying for.
And IKEA is stuck in a price war with rival mail-order firms. Every cut is answered with a deeper one... and quality starts to slip.
Customers start to doubt that anything this cheap can be any good.
Ingvar has a choice. Keep cutting... or find another way.
In 1953, he turns an old carpentry factory in the small town of Almhult into a showroom.
For the first time, customers can sit on the chairs, open the drawers... and compare quality and price with their own eyes.
People come from all over Sweden to see it. Trust is back. But moving bulky furniture is still expensive... and that's where our table returns.
IKEA's catalogue photographer is a young man named Gillis Lundgren... the company's fourth employee.
He's trying to get a little leaf-shaped table called Lövet into his small car, for a catalogue photo shoot. It won't fit.
So he takes the legs off... and lays them flat under the tabletop.
To be fair... IKEA didn't invent flat-pack. Chairs were shipped flat back in the eighteen-hundreds.
But this is the moment it stopped being a trick... and became the whole business model.
Flat furniture takes far less space in trucks and warehouses. It's cheaper to ship... cheaper to store... and later, customers carry it home themselves.
Or, as people at IKEA like to put it... there's no point in shipping air.
In 1958, the first IKEA store opens in Almhult. At the time, it's billed as the biggest furniture showroom in Scandinavia.
In one corner, there's a little coffee stand. Two years later, it's a real restaurant... the start of a food business that will one day sell meatballs worldwide.
Lower costs mean lower prices. And low prices have been making IKEA some powerful enemies.

parts.title_ru: Часть 3 — бойкот, рост, тёмная сторона и финал

beats.text: In fact, IKEA has been making enemies for years. Sweden's furniture retailers are furious about its low prices.
They get IKEA banned from a Stockholm trade fair... and they warn suppliers: sell to Ingvar, and we stop buying from you.
So Ingvar gets creative. Some suppliers quietly sell to him under other names.
But the boycott bites. By 1961, IKEA simply can't get enough furniture from Swedish factories.
So in January 1961, Ingvar travels to communist Poland... and starts ordering furniture from Polish factories, where costs are far lower.
Buy cheap, sell cheap. The farm boy's trick, all over again. The boycott that was meant to kill IKEA... ends up making it even cheaper.
In 1963, IKEA opens its first store outside Sweden, near Oslo, in Norway. Then Denmark.
In 1973, Switzerland, the first IKEA outside Scandinavia. Then Germany, which becomes its biggest market. And then, the world.
At the end of the seventies, Gillis Lundgren, the man who took the legs off that table, sketches a bookcase on a paper napkin. It's called Billy.
It becomes one of the best-selling pieces of furniture ever made. More than a hundred and twenty million sold, by IKEA's own count.
Today, IKEA has around five hundred big stores, and hundreds of smaller ones... with more than nine hundred million visits a year.
But the story isn't spotless.
In the seventies and eighties, political prisoners in East Germany worked in factories making furniture and parts for IKEA.
In 2012, after an independent investigation, IKEA admitted it... and that some of its staff were aware prisoners might be used. It said it deeply regretted it.
In 2024, IKEA Germany pledged six million euros to a German fund for victims of the East German regime.

Environmental group Earthsight has also alleged that wood from illegal logging in Ukraine and Siberia ended up in IKEA products. IKEA said its wood was legal... but stopped buying from some suppliers.
And its founder had a past of his own. As a young man, in and after wartime Sweden, Ingvar was involved with a pro-Nazi movement.
When it came out in 1994, he wrote to his staff that it was the greatest mistake of his life.

Ingvar Kamprad died in 2018, at ninety-one. A complicated man... and a famously frugal one. Often ranked among the richest people on the planet, he flew economy and drove the same old Volvo for years.
So, back to our question. How does a farm boy with a box of matches build all this?
Not with one genius idea. With a boy who bought in bulk and sold cheap... a showroom people could touch... and a table without its legs.
Every time the world said no... the price war, the trade fair, the boycott... IKEA found a cheaper, simpler way.
And that's how they built IKEA.
Next time... another company that started with almost nothing. It's on your screen right now. And if you want every new story... subscribe. I'm Mila Sterling... see you in the next one.

beats.text: This is why IKEA sells furniture in flat boxes.
In the mid-fifties, IKEA employee Gillis Lundgren couldn't fit a little table into his car for a photo shoot.
So he took the legs off.
IKEA didn't invent flat-pack... but that tiny fix became its whole business model.
Flat furniture is cheaper to ship, cheaper to store... and you carry it home yourself.
Why pay to ship air?
Follow for more stories of how they built it. And remember...
IKEA isn't a made-up word. It's a home address.
I and K... Ingvar Kamprad, the founder. E... Elmtaryd, the farm where he grew up. A... Agunnaryd, the nearby village.
He registered the company in 1943, at just seventeen.
He was still a minor... so first he cycled to his guardian for a signature.
The man couldn't see why a boy needed a company... but he signed.
Follow for more stories of how they built it. Because now you know...
Swedish furniture sellers once tried to destroy IKEA.
In the nineteen-fifties, they were furious about its low prices. They got IKEA banned from a Stockholm trade fair...
and warned suppliers: sell to IKEA, and we stop buying from you.
Some suppliers sold to it anyway, under other names.
Then, in 1961, Ingvar went to communist Poland... where furniture was even cheaper to make.
The boycott meant to kill IKEA... made it stronger.
Follow for more stories of how they built it. That's what happened when...
Why does IKEA lead you through a maze... then feed you meatballs?
First, the food. Families drove from all over Sweden to the very first store... and they arrived hungry.
Ingvar figured a hungry customer is hard to do business with. So in 1960, IKEA opened a restaurant.
The meatballs came in 1985. Now? Over a billion a year.
And the maze? It began in 1965, at a round store near Stockholm inspired by New York's Guggenheim Museum. It walks you past every room...
Follow for more stories of how they built it. Next time you're lost in there...

packaging.description_body:
In the mid-1950s, an IKEA employee couldn't fit a little table into his car, so he took the legs off. That small moment helped turn a farm boy's mail-order business into the world's biggest furniture brand.

From selling matches as a five-year-old in Småland to a milk lorry that delivered his first parcels, a price war, a boycott that backfired and the Billy bookcase, this is how IKEA was built. We also cover the chapters IKEA has had to answer for: East German prison labour, wood sourcing and its founder's past.

**Картинок 53 + фон обложки**: кадры 01–40 остаются под своими номерами, 25 = две картинки (25a и 25b), новые кадры — 41, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 55, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 54. Помечены {{НОВЫЙ}} и {{ИЗМЕНЁН}}.

**Из промптов убраны** годы, бумаги с текстом и вывески, из-за которых модель рисует буквы. Внешность героев описана одинаково во всех кадрах.

steps: **Озвучка — 7 файлов.** Каждую часть из «Текста озвучки» вставляй в Syntx целиком и отдельно: part1, part2, part3. Затем 4 Shorts: short1…short4. Если сервис режет по длине — part1a, part1b и т.д.
**Проба стиля — кадры 01 и 05** (05 — с фото Mila). Пришли мне. Если стиль и лицо нравятся — генерируй остальные.
**Остальные кадры — всего 53 картинок** по списку ниже, формат 16:9. Имя файла = номер кадра: 07.png, 25a.png, 41.png. Неудачный кадр просто перегенерируй, сверять каждый со мной не нужно.
**Фон обложки** — промпт «thumbnail» в конце списка, файл thumbnail.png.
**Kling (по желанию)** — 7 кадров, картинка → видео 5 сек. Имя файла = номер кадра: 10.mp4.
**Отправка** — всё одной папкой: 7 mp3 + 53 картинок + thumbnail.png (+ клипы Kling).
